title: Eli’s Sons Were Priests—and Scripture Accuses Them of Sleeping With Women at the Tabernacle Entrance
paragraphs: Eli’s Sons Were Priests—and Scripture Accuses Them of Sleeping With Women at the Tabernacle Entrance

They wore the priesthood. They handled holy sacrifices. They stood near the presence of God. But Scripture says something terrifying about Hophni and Phinehas before it ever tells us about the women: “They did not know the LORD.” And that may be the most frightening sentence in their entire story.
Imagine walking toward the tabernacle at Shiloh.
You came carrying a sacrifice.

Maybe you were grieving. Maybe you had sinned. Maybe your family desperately needed God. Maybe you had traveled for miles because somewhere inside you was still the hope that when you came near the place associated with His presence, you would find mercy.
Smoke rises.
Animals are being prepared.
Prayers are being whispered.
The name of the LORD is being invoked.
And standing there are priests.
Hophni and Phinehas.
Sons of Eli.
Men born into a sacred family, serving around sacred things, occupying sacred positions.
From a distance, everything might have looked religious.
Then Scripture pulls back the curtain.
And what it reveals should frighten anyone who has ever confused being around God with actually knowing God.
“Now the sons of Eli were sons of Belial; they knew not the LORD.” — 1 Samuel 2:12, KJV
The Hebrew is even more arresting:
וּבְנֵי עֵלִי בְּנֵי בְלִיָּעַל לֹא יָדְעוּ אֶת־יְהוָה
Uvenei ‘Eli benei veliyya‘al; lo yade‘u et-YHWH.
The crucial words are בְּנֵי בְלִיָּעַל — benei veliyya‘al: literally, “sons of worthlessness,” an expression describing thoroughly corrupt or worthless men.
Then comes the diagnosis beneath the scandal:
לֹא יָדְעוּ אֶת־יְהוָה — lo yade‘u et-YHWH.
“They did not know YHWH.”
Read that again.
They were priests.
And they did not know the LORD.
That is the horror of this story.
Their greatest problem was not merely sexual sin.
It was not merely greed.
It was not merely abuse of religious privilege.
Beneath everything was a catastrophic absence of genuine knowledge of God.
They knew religious procedure.
They knew sacrifices.
They knew priestly privilege.
They knew how the system worked.
They apparently knew enough about holy things to exploit them.
But Scripture says they did not know the One to whom all those holy things belonged.
And suddenly this ancient scandal becomes uncomfortable.
Because it is possible to know Christian vocabulary and not know Christ.
Possible to raise your hands during worship while hiding what those hands touched last night.
Possible to post Bible verses while secretly feeding an addiction.
Possible to preach grace while refusing repentance.
Possible to carry a title that says “minister,” “pastor,” “leader,” “Christian,” or “believer” while living as though the eyes of God cannot penetrate a locked room.
Hophni and Phinehas are not preserved in Scripture merely so modern Christians can stare at two wicked men from thousands of years ago.
Their story is a mirror.
And mirrors become uncomfortable when we stop looking at everyone else.

The biblical account says these priests were already corrupting the sacrificial system. They took portions of offerings improperly and demanded meat before the fat had been offered to God. When worshipers resisted, their servants threatened force.
Think about what that means.
People were coming to worship God, and God's representatives were making obedience harder.
People brought sacrifices, and priests exploited them.
The sanctuary had become an opportunity for appetite.
Scripture therefore says:
“Wherefore the sin of the young men was very great before the LORD: for men abhorred the offering of the LORD.” — 1 Samuel 2:17, KJV
That sentence is devastating.
Their behavior did not remain private.
Their corruption damaged other people's relationship with worship.
And this is why spiritual hypocrisy is never as private as the hypocrite imagines.
When someone uses the name of God to feed greed, lust, ego, control, or appetite, people can begin associating the ugliness of the representative with the character of the God supposedly represented.
Some people reading this know exactly what that feels like.
Perhaps someone who spoke about Jesus wounded you.
Perhaps someone carrying a Bible manipulated you.
Perhaps a church leader betrayed your trust.
Perhaps somebody used spiritual authority to get what they wanted and then expected everyone else to remain silent to “protect the ministry.”
Scripture does not protect Hophni and Phinehas by hiding what they did.
God had their corruption written down.
That matters.
Then comes 1 Samuel 2:22.

Eli was old, and the text reports that he heard what his sons were doing throughout Israel, including the accusation that they were lying with the women serving at the entrance of the tent of meeting.
The traditional Hebrew textual form underlying many familiar translations reads of the women:
הַנָּשִׁים הַצֹּבְאוֹת פֶּתַח אֹהֶל מוֹעֵד
hannashim hatzove’ot petach ohel mo‘ed—
the women serving or assembling at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting.
And Scripture says Eli heard that his sons יִשְׁכְּבוּן — yishkevun, “were lying/sleeping,” with them.
This is why many translations straightforwardly render the accusation as Hophni and Phinehas sleeping with, lying with, or having sexual relations with these women.

There is, however, an important textual caution for careful Bible readers: the sexual accusation in this verse has a manuscript/textual-history complication, and some textual witnesses and modern translations do not include that clause. So we should not pretend there is no textual question here.
But neither should we soften the portrait Scripture unquestionably gives us.

Even apart from that disputed clause, Hophni and Phinehas are explicitly described as corrupt men who did not know the LORD, who abused the sacrificial system, treated the LORD's offering with contempt, ignored correction, and eventually came under divine judgment.
The Bible is not presenting misunderstood religious celebrities.
It is presenting corrupt priests.
And notice where the alleged sexual corruption occurs.
At the entrance to the Tent of Meeting.
Near the place associated with worship.
Near sacrifice.
Near prayer.
Near holiness.
That juxtaposition is almost unbearable.
Holy place.
Unholy appetite.
Priestly clothing.
Corrupt hearts.
Religious proximity.
Spiritual estrangement.
And perhaps that is exactly where this story finds us.
Because sin rarely announces itself by saying, “I intend to destroy you.”
It whispers.
Just once.
Nobody knows.
You deserve this.
You can repent later.
You're still serving God.
You're still attending church.
You're still reading Scripture.
You're still posting Christian content.
You're still helping people.
Surely everything between you and God cannot be that bad.
Hophni and Phinehas stand forever in Scripture as evidence that proximity to holy things cannot substitute for holiness of heart.
You can stand near the altar and still be far from God.
You can know worship songs and not worship.
You can explain theology and refuse the Lordship of Christ.
You can fool a congregation.
You can fool followers.
You can fool your spouse.
You can fool your parents.
You can fool the person sitting beside you on Sunday.
But you cannot fool God.
And perhaps somebody reading this has grown exhausted from trying.
Exhausted from deleting evidence.
Exhausted from clearing browser histories.
Exhausted from pretending the marriage is fine.
Exhausted from preaching convictions you stopped practicing privately.
Exhausted from saying, “I'm okay.”
Exhausted from promising God, “This is the last time.”
Then falling again.
And again.
And again.
Listen carefully.
The lesson of Hophni and Phinehas is not that sinners are beyond mercy.
If that were the Gospel, none of us could stand.
The warning is what happens when sinners continually harden themselves against the God who confronts their sin.
Eli confronted his sons.
“Why do ye such things? for I hear of your evil dealings by all this people.” — 1 Samuel 2:23, KJV.
But they would not listen.
That detail changes everything.
God's confrontation was not an invitation to improve their image.
It was a summons to turn.
And they refused.
There is an enormous difference between struggling against sin and making peace with it.
Between falling and deciding the floor is home.
Between crying, “God, have mercy on me,” and saying, “God has no right to tell me what to do.”
Repentance does not mean you have never fallen.
Repentance means that when God exposes what is killing you, you stop defending it and turn toward Him.
This is where the story becomes more than scandal.
Because Hophni and Phinehas are not the final priests in the Bible.
Another Priest was coming.
Not corrupt.
Not predatory.
Not greedy.
Not exploiting worshipers.
Not taking sacrifices for Himself.
He would become the sacrifice.
Jesus Christ.

The New Testament presents Him as our great High Priest, holy and undefiled, the One who entered not through the blood of animals but through His own sacrificial work and who is able to save completely those who draw near to God through Him.
Where corrupt religious men take from people, Jesus gives Himself for people.
Where corrupt priests use sacred office to satisfy appetite, Jesus lays down His life.
Where sinners dishonor God's holiness, Jesus fulfills righteousness.
Where guilty people deserve judgment, Christ bears sin at the cross.
And where scandal seems to have written the final chapter, grace picks up the pen.
That is the Gospel.
Not that your sin was insignificant.
Not that God shrugged at what happened.
Not that holiness stopped mattering.
Grace is infinitely more beautiful than that.
At Calvary, God did not pretend sin was cheap.
The cross declares how serious sin actually is.
And simultaneously, how astonishingly far divine love went to rescue sinners.
“For Christ also hath once suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God.” — 1 Peter 3:18, KJV.
The Just for the unjust.
The Holy for the unholy.
The innocent Christ for guilty sinners.
That means your secret does not have to become your identity.
Your pornography does not have to write your ending.
Your adultery does not have to write your ending.
Your hypocrisy does not have to write your ending.
Your greed does not have to write your ending.
Your pride does not have to write your ending.
Your years of pretending do not have to write your ending.
But grace is not permission to continue hiding.
Jesus does not rescue us so that we can decorate our chains with Christian language.
He calls us out of darkness.
Confess.
Repent.
Bring the hidden thing into the light before the hidden thing devours what remains.

If you have harmed someone, repentance may require more than tears. It may require confession, accountability, restitution where appropriate, surrendering authority, accepting consequences, and seeking help. Grace does not mean victims must pretend nothing happened, and forgiveness must never be weaponized to silence those who have been harmed.
Christ's grace is not camouflage for corruption.
It is rescue from corruption.
Maybe this article did not reach you because you needed another interesting Bible story.
Maybe you needed the frightening sentence:
“They did not know the LORD.”
You know church.
But do you know Him?
You know Christian content.
But do you know Him?
You know what to say when someone asks whether you're saved.
But when nobody is watching...
do you know Him?
Not merely facts about Jesus.
Jesus.
The crucified and risen Son of God.
The Savior who receives repentant sinners.
The Lord who refuses to leave His people enslaved to what He died to redeem them from.
But do not run from conviction either.
And if Christ has already pulled you out of something you once thought would destroy you, tell enough of your testimony to give somebody else hope.
Someone reading the comments may desperately need evidence that Jesus still restores people.
Not because anyone can purchase God's blessing.
And never because giving money earns salvation.
It cannot.
We support Gospel work because grace has already been freely given to us in Christ, and because we want biblical truth to continue reaching people who desperately need it.
Because somewhere tonight there is another person standing frighteningly close to holy things while drifting farther from the Holy One.
Maybe they still sing.
Maybe they still preach.
Maybe they still serve.
Maybe nobody suspects anything.
Maybe that person is reading these words.
Hophni and Phinehas teach us that a title cannot save you.
An altar cannot save you.
A religious family cannot save you.
A ministry cannot save you.
Your reputation cannot save you.
Only Jesus saves.
So stop protecting the version of yourself that Christ is calling you to crucify.
Bring the scandal into the light.
Bring the addiction.
Bring the lust.
Bring the betrayal.
Bring the hypocrisy.
Bring the shame.
Bring the thing you swore nobody would ever know.
Bring it to Jesus.
Not because sin does not matter.
But because the blood of Christ is the only reason your sin does not have to speak the final word.
The sons of Eli stood near an altar while their hearts wandered from God.
Jesus climbed onto a cross so wandering hearts could come home.
And perhaps the most unforgettable truth you can carry away from this story is this:
Your scandal may explain how you arrived at the cross—but it does not get to decide who walks away from it. Jesus does.
Because the goal was never merely to look religious.
The goal is to know Him.
